name: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors

clinicalPearls: Cardiac tumors are broadly divided into primary tumors (arising in the heart) and metastatic tumors from a distant source; metastatic involvement is far more common and is seen in up to roughly 20% of patients with end-stage metastatic cancer.

Primary cardiac tumors are rare (about 1 in 2000 in autopsy series); roughly three-quarters are histologically benign, and most of those benign tumors are myxomas, while malignant primaries (almost all sarcomas) make up about 25%.

Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, comprising one-third to one-half of cases at postmortem and about three-quarters of surgically treated tumors; it favors the third through sixth decades with a female predilection.

Roughly 90% of myxomas are sporadic; the remainder are familial (autosomal dominant), often as part of the Carney complex (cardiac/skin/breast myxomas, lentigines or pigmented nevi, and endocrine overactivity), associated in about 70% of cases with inactivating mutations in the PRKAR1A tumor-suppressor gene.

Sporadic myxomas are typically solitary, pedunculated on a fibrovascular stalk, and arise from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis, most often in the left atrium; familial/syndromic myxomas occur in younger patients, are often multiple, may be ventricular, and recur more often.

Myxomas most commonly produce obstructive features mimicking mitral valve disease (stenosis from prolapse into the mitral orifice, or regurgitation from valvular trauma); symptoms may be sudden or positional because of gravitational effects on tumor position.
A characteristic low-pitched early or mid-diastolic 'tumor plop' may be heard, attributed to the tumor striking the mitral valve or ventricular wall.

Myxomas can cause peripheral or pulmonary embolic events (tumor fragments or associated thrombus) and constitutional/cytokine-mediated features (often interleukin-6), so they are frequently misdiagnosed as endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome.

Papillary fibroelastomas are the most common tumors of the cardiac valves (friable, frond-like, usually solitary) and, although often silent, may embolize to cause TIA, stroke, or myocardial infarction.

Rhabdomyomas and fibromas are the most common cardiac tumors of infants and children, usually ventricular; rhabdomyomas occur in about 50% of children with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations) and tend to regress, whereas fibromas (PTCH1) tend to grow.

Malignant primaries are almost all sarcomas (angiosarcoma most common in adults, rhabdomyosarcoma in children), frequently right-sided, rapidly growing, and often invade the pericardium; about one-third are metastatic at diagnosis, usually to the lungs.

Tissue histology remains the gold standard for diagnosis; echocardiography is the usual initial test, with cardiac MRI (gadolinium) helping differentiate tumor from thrombus and benign from malignant lesions.
harrison.pathophysiology: Cardiac tumors are classified as primary (benign, chiefly myxoma; or malignant, chiefly sarcoma) or secondary/metastatic. Myxomas are gelatinous masses of myxoma cells in a glycosaminoglycan-rich stroma, usually arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis and most often projecting into the left atrium on a fibrovascular stalk. Clinical effects arise from three mechanisms: mechanical obstruction or valvular interference (mimicking mitral stenosis/regurgitation, or outflow obstruction for ventricular tumors), embolization of tumor fragments or associated thrombus, and constitutional effects from tumor-secreted cytokines such as interleukin-6. Familial myxomas relate to PRKAR1A inactivation within the Carney complex. Metastatic tumors reach the heart by hematogenous or lymphangitic spread or direct invasion, most often involving the pericardium, then myocardium of any chamber, and rarely the endocardium or valves.
additionalDifferentials: Subaortic or subpulmonic (outflow tract) stenosis from a ventricular tumor
Restrictive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (mimicked by pediatric rhabdomyoma/fibroma)
infectionMimics: Infective endocarditis (myxoma with embolic phenomena, fever, and constitutional symptoms is frequently misdiagnosed as endocarditis)
nonInfectiousMimics: Myocardial hypertrophy mistaken for a mass
Collagen vascular disease (mimicked by myxoma constitutional/laboratory picture)
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography (initial modality; tumor location, size, attachment site, impact on valves/pericardium)
Transesophageal echocardiography (improved characterization and spatial resolution; aids surgical planning)
Cardiac MRI with gadolinium (tissue characterization, local invasion, differentiating tumor from thrombus)
Gated cardiac CT (anatomic and tissue assessment, calcified lesions, extracardiac involvement; useful when MRI not feasible)
Nuclear imaging including FDG-PET (extracardiac disease; some tumor types) and 131I-MIBG scanning for paraganglioma
Echocardiographic screening of first-degree relatives when myxoma is familial/syndromic
Pericardiocentesis with cytology for malignant pericardial effusion (reported sensitivity ~67-92%)
redFlags: Syncope or positional symptoms suggesting intermittent obstruction by a mobile tumor
Embolic events (stroke, TIA, peripheral or pulmonary embolism) as the presenting feature
Cardiac tamponade or large pericardial effusion (especially with metastatic disease)
Rapidly progressive heart failure or chamber/vena caval obstruction suggesting sarcoma
New heart block or conduction disturbance (tumors near the AV node, e.g., hemangioma/mesothelioma, can cause sudden death)
harrison.prognosis: Benign myxoma is generally cured by surgical excision; recurrence is about 1-2% in sporadic cases but 12-22% in familial cases (multifocal disease or incomplete resection). Malignant primary tumors carry a poor prognosis: sarcomas typically progress rapidly to death within weeks to months from hemodynamic compromise, local invasion, or metastasis, and respond poorly to radiotherapy/chemotherapy. The notable exception is primary cardiac lymphoma, the most chemotherapy-sensitive primary cardiac malignancy, with long-term survival in about 40% of treated patients. Metastatic cardiac involvement usually occurs with advanced disease, is clinically apparent only about 10% of the time, is rarely the cause of death, and carries an overall poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing myxoma as infective endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome because of fever, embolism, and laboratory abnormalities (e.g., elevated ESR/CRP, anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia).
Catheterizing the chamber harboring a tumor, which risks tumor embolization; angiography/catheterization is no longer mandatory when noninvasive imaging is adequate and coronary disease is unlikely.
Failing to screen first-degree relatives of young patients with multiple myxomas or syndromic features.
Attributing cardiac symptoms in cancer patients solely to the tumor when radiotherapy/chemotherapy-induced myocarditis, pericarditis, or cardiomyopathy can produce identical findings.
Overlooking that a left-sided sarcoma may be mistaken for a myxoma.
